title: A Telomerase Inhibitor Revealed
body_text: Here’s a very nice structural biology paper on an important target, telomerase. This has become a famous enzyme over the years because of its role in maintaining a crucial part of chromosomal structure, the eponymous telomeres. Those are the “end caps” of chormosomes, and it’s not surprising that they come in for some special treatment. Just leaving open reading frames out there seems like an invitation for trouble (from several possible mechanisms), and evolution has apparently come to that conclusion itself. What you find are repetitive base sequences, ending in a single-stranded “overhang” on the 3’ strand, which is associated with a particular group of “shelterin” proteins. This is a very deep feature, found across vertebrates, plants, insects, protozoans, fungi, you name it. So far, so good, but it’s long been noted that this structure does not get completely replicated every time a cell divides - in fact, the telomeres shorten every time, and without something to counteract this things would reach a hard stop at some point. This was recognized by the Soviet biologist Alexey Olovnikov back in the 1970s, who really should have shared in the 2009 Nobel Prize in this area (an unfortunate example of the limits of the three-scientists-at-most provisions of the Nobel will). That counteracting force is (mainly) telomerase, an enzyme that Olovnikov predicted must exist even though no one had seen it at the time. It’s a mixed RNA/amino acid ribonuclear protein (known as TER) that sits in a complex assembly with a telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) along with a histone protein dimer and another associated ribonuclear protein (H/ACA) complex. What all this handles is the addition of multiple fresh telomere sequence repeats to that 3’ overhang after a DNA replication event. But this only happens in particular types of cells. Ordinary cells don’t seem to have any telomerase activity at all, and they indeed are counting down the telomere clock every time they divide. It’s things like stem cells and germline cells that keep resetting with telomerase. . .and the huge majority of cancer cells too. It makes a horrible sort of sense. Tumor cells are generally rapidly dividing, and would just as rapidly run out of telomere space if things were normal, with all sorts of fatal DNA damage to follow. But tumor cells that survive have upregulated their telomerase expression to keep the party going, and that has made it a widely-recognized oncology target. The role of telomerase in cancer cells is a story that’s been getting more complicated every year, but people are plunging ahead, as the terrifyingly long list in this paper will illustrate. Small molecules, oligonucleotides, gene therapy, ribozymes, immunotherapy - every weapon you can think of is being brought to bear on numerous working parts of the whole machinery. So far, none of these have shown the benefits that people have hoped for in the clinic, not least due to the induction of backup methods of telomere lengthening. One drug (imetelstat) has been approved so far, but there’s a lot that we don’t know. That lack of knowledge in what is a very complicated situation is why you shouldn't believe anyone who tells. you that telomerase activity is the Key To All Cancer or the Key to All Aging. It's very important, no doubt about it, but this is some truly deep biology and full of billions of years of complications. One of the big foci has been a compound called BIBR1532, a small-molecule inhibitor of human TERT. That one’s been around for over twenty years now, but the paper linked in the first sentence of this post finally shows us in detail how it binds! And these results contradict the most widely-accepted binding model that people had been using up until now, which placed the molecule out on a region of TERT called the C-extension domain. That was based on a crystal structure of the compound bound to an insect telomerase, and the authors were say that these results “probably hampered subsequent drug optimization efforts”. I’d say they’re right - some of the compounds made from working off those earlier data actually seem to have made binding to this hidden pocket more unlikely! Instead, the cryo-EM data with the human proteins show it in a (previously unrecognized) deep pocket between the “finger” and “palm” regions of the protein. The authors have a variety of single-particle structures at various stages of the enzymatic process, and what they find is that the inhibitor doesn’t cause the overall telomerase structure to change much. But what it does do is mess up the process of adding each new nucleotide to the telomeres themselves through an allosteric mechanism. This will surely set off new rounds of compound modeling and optimization to see if these structural insights can be turned into more potent drug candidates. I wish everyone involved luck, and I’m glad to see the increased clarity that this paper provides. But I fear that the downstream biology is lying in wait for all of these ideas (those alternative telomere-lengthening processes, for example, along with who knows what else). But better compounds are a way to start finding this stuff out!
